The participants were Nepali fiction writer Neelam Karki Niharika, travel writer Krishna Bajgai and my former student and well-known scholar Mahesh Paudyal. Sangita Swechcha curated the webinar.

Diasporic writing has become a popular subject among writers within and outside Nepal, even though it may require further discussion and writing to conclude that it has transformed Nepali writing. Discussions of the Nepali diaspora encompass both broad and minuscule issues. Debates about the role of the Nepali diaspora, especially in Darjeeling, Sikkim, Assam and other places, have undergone various metamorphoses throughout history. Nepalis and their role in contributing to the formation of states and territorial administrations in India have gone down in history.

The first phase of diaspora is one of ambivalence. Literary writers of the early generations, all based and active in Darjeeling, expressed ambivalence in their writing and in their shifting bases between India and Nepal. The pioneers known by the acronym Su Dha Pa or Surya Bikram Gyawali, Dharanidhar Sharma and Paras Mani Pradhan represent that diasporic ambivalence in Nepali writing and activism. Surya Bikram Gyawali became the writer of ‘brave Nepali history’ (in the words of historian Pratyoush Onta) and the Chancellor of the Royal Nepal Academy. Dharanidhar moved to Nepal.

Literature has played a quiet role. Obtrusive and unobtrusive modes can be identified in this regard. Lain Singh Bangdel’s position was similar to Gyawali’s. Bangdel also became Chancellor of the Royal Nepal Academy, but his famous diasporic novel Muluk Bahira, or ‘outside the native land ’, pulsates with ambivalence and a quest for diasporic identity. Lil Bahadur Chetri’s Basain has become a classic of migration literature, as the title suggests. Many examples exist.

The fuzzy border of diaspora should be noted here. Literature production in Banaras became possible through ‘print capitalism’, to use Francesca Orseni’s expression, in the second half of the 19th century and continued well into the early decades of the 20th century. This deserves discussion in relation to diasporic literature. Production, readership and sales were the words of print capitalism. The printing of Bhanubhakta Acharya’s Ramayana brings together these various strands of the early diasporic anxieties. The mantra of the early Indic Nepali diaspora was the quest, and its primary means was producing texts. Banaras’ print capitalism saw the publication of many books and literary magazines. Then came the literary textbook production of Paras Mani Pradhan. The carefully prepared diasporic texts were our textbooks. I grew up with them without ever thinking about who had created and produced them.

So what I call the productive ambivalence of books from the first phase of the Indic Nepali diaspora was part of the educational campaign. We should look at this with a broader perspective. The fuzzy lines between native and diasporic literature remained a force of a certain order for a long time. They persisted well into the writings of Indra Rai and the Tesro Ayam. The diasporic line became broader. Later, the idioms changed. Literary writers became Indian Nepali writers. The motif of the ‘muluk bahira’ psyche was not strongly evoked even in earlier times. Govinda Bhattarai’s novel Muglan is an important intervention in that area. Written by a Nepali writer with diasporic sympathy and empathy, this novel evokes Muglan’s conditionality. I would call it an important meta-fictional work on the theme of diasporic imaginaire.

Ramji Timilsina, a fine scholar and my erstwhile student and a PhD on diasporic literature, in an article titled ‘Use and Misuse of ‘Diaspora’ in Nepali Literary Discourse’ says, “Those who have crossed the border of Nepal, have permanently settled in a new nation, and have grown a community that resembles and reflects Nepal are the members of the Nepali Diaspora.” He further adds, “They maintain and grow contacts and relations with the homeland through its members and make physical visits to it; they make use of communication”. Timilsina concludes, “These features show that a diaspora is different from transnational mobile communities and the transnational outsiders.”

Literary critics and historians assert that the geographical and national spaces of the Nepali Diaspora are in India, Bhutan and Burma. The other category of the incipient Nepali Diaspora, as commonly discussed, is England, USA, Canada and Australia. Nepali diaspora is growing. But we must address the earlier category again. I have heard in interactions and read in writings that the ambivalence of the Nepali diaspora in the case of the Nepalis in India is evoked frequently. We ask: Are the established Indian Nepali writers diasporic? I think they are Indian Nepali writers. They do not maintain the nostalgia or angst related to the original land in the same way as writers of earlier times.

The question of readership in diasporic literature is important; it deserves serious discussion and engagement. This calls for expanding readership and working with a psyche of sharing. I think this is already happening and should be seen as an important shift in readership and in the creation of a readership sphere in different countries. The growing diasporic population, rising interest in writing, and the availability of sharing tools are notable. I think this phenomenon has become an important reality that will affect the very nature of diasporic literature and the praxis of sharing and spreading.

Another feature is the careful and subtle creation of the diasporic experience by native writers and publishing them either in the original language, such as Nepali and Nepal Bhasha, or getting them translated into English. I want to mention one such novel titled 17 September written in Nepal Bhasha by Malla K Sundar and translated into English by the Lisbon-based scholar Jyoti Tuladhar.

Nepali diasporic literary output is growing. The spheres of writing are expanding. With this, the identification of diasporic Nepali writings and writers is also growing. Connectivity and organisational networks have created a unique condition in diasporic literature. Literary organisations like the International Nepali Literary Society (Anesasa), along with visits by writers from Nepal to other countries, have fostered a culture of connectivity that encourages diasporic literature. Efforts are made to build cross-national readership by familiarising readers with works by diasporic writers. Launching their work in Nepal, especially in Kathmandu, organising interactions with them and creating literary awards are some productive activities.

articles.title: The state kept only one copy
articles.summary:
Every person who has waited in a malpot (Land Registration) office for a copy of lalpurja (Land Ownership Certificate) knows that moment. Someone walks into the back room and comes out with the sresta, a ledger too heavy to fit flat on the table. He dips his thumb in water, flips through pages and locates your record. Whatever is written, there is the truth about your land, as far as the state cares. Since those ledgers were burned in the Gen Z protests of September, all the land transactions in some districts just ceased, waiting for someone to recreate a ledger again, one owner at a time.

Last week, the Auditor General Toyam Raya told the Public Accounts Committee how much we lost. Records of 179 public bodies were destroyed during the protests of September 8-9. Around Rs148 billion worth of government transactions never got audited because of this. It can be recollected from the banks’ statements and government software, but the proof of whether it was done legally was burned down.

His deputy, Deepak Lamichhane, pointed out that the records could be reconstructed using the general vouchers that survived and internal audit reports. Reconstruction sounds like a lot, but lawmakers sitting in that room dismissed any notion that an office cannot be audited due to loss of papers.

My field is governed by a rule known as 3-2-1. Every piece of information you cannot afford to lose should have three copies, two kinds of storage, and one of them should be in another place altogether. It is not smart, and it is not novel, but this is exactly why every serious laboratory follows it without a thought. The rule assumes that the building will be destroyed, but does not bother speculating how.

Nepal followed this rule in one place, and it saved us. The Integrated Data Management Centre is located in Singha Durbar. While the fires ravaged other buildings around it, the centre came through unharmed, and its recovery site in Hetauda was never threatened. “The country would have gone blank,” said Manish Bhattarai, who runs that centre. He was not overstating. This building stores the information of Nepal Rastra Bank, the Home Ministry and police databases, company registry, Nagarik App and websites of all 753 local governments.

The same logic saved the land records. An estimate suggests that a million land documents burned in those two days, but people can still reclaim what belongs to them thanks to the existence of this information in the central system. Investment Board Nepal lost its own servers and hard disks in that fire, but it managed to preserve its files because they were stored at that centre and not in its own building.

The Supreme Court had no such arrangement. Basic details of the cases, such as party names and case numbers, were kept digitally, but the files themselves were paper-based. Roughly 20,000 pending case files and a far greater number of those with verdicts issued were burned. For several months, the court has been restoring this information by publishing notices urging litigants and their lawyers to come with photocopies of their files. Over 17,000 were restored by July. The real backup, it turns out, was hiding in photocopy shops outside the courthouse gates.

This is the thing that worries me. In the budget, a sovereign AI compute centre was announced, tentatively in Syuchatar, and the purchase of thousands of processors to operate it. I was arguing for it, and I still do. But no model is as good as the records it relies upon. Two days before this announcement, The Kathmandu Post reported that government servers were malfunctioning all over the country and that a single software breakdown took land revenue offices offline in all 77 districts. Most government data centres’ servers are seven or eight years old and have already reached the point where nobody can support them anymore. We plan to compute on the data we have no idea how to save.

During the same hearing, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle promised the government will digitise government records and follow any instruction issued by the committee. Nobody offered a deadline. Nobody asked who will audit it. There is still no rule requiring every ordinary district office, ward office or school to store a copy of its records in another place.

The usual objection to this idea is the cost. Half of it is legitimate. Digitising millions of pages is a very slow and expensive process, as the Supreme Court discovered for itself this year. Holding a second copy of information already digitised is not. Storing it costs a bit more now than it used to, because of the current worldwide rush into AI which pushed memory prices sharply up. It is nothing compared to the cost of importing processors.

Underneath all of this lurks the question of what people get away with. Once the records of 179 public bodies disappear, the proof of any questionable information they contained disappears with them. I am not suggesting that someone set the building on fire to hide a ledger. I am saying that we created a state in which such an excuse becomes permanently available.

There will be speeches about rebuilding next month. It is easy to buy some furniture. Nobody said anything about the srestha in the backroom, and until someone does it, the next fire will cost us the same as this one.

articles.title: Trump orders Pentagon to cut back military exercises with South Korea
articles.summary:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday instructed the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” 10 days of joint military exercises with ‌South Korea as they were about to get underway, citing the cost of the drills and Seoul’s refusal to take part in actions against Iran.

Hours before exercises were scheduled to begin, Trump said on his Truth Social site that although it was too late to cancel the drills entirely, he was “not happy” that the US had previously agreed to participate and highlighted his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

“These exercises are not only costly... but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Trump wrote.

The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises are scheduled to run from August 17 to 27, with about 18,000 South Korean military ⁠personnel participating. The drills are expected to include operations to counter drones, disrupt GPS signals and cyberattacks to adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities, officials said last week.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff told Reuters that the drills started on Monday as scheduled, but declined comment on Trump’s comments. The country’s presidential office and defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond on a public holiday in Seoul.

A Pentagon spokesperson referred questions on the matter to the White House, which did not immediately respond to a request for more information on next steps for the drills.

Up-and-down relationship

Trump has long sought to end or curtail military exercises with South Korea, going back to his first term, calling them “provocative” and costly. He has also clashed with Seoul over sharing the costs of stationing 28,500 US troops in South Korea and their role in securing the broader region.

Pyongyang routinely denounces the US-South Korean exercises as preparations for an invasion. North Korea last Wednesday fired a ballistic missile from its eastern coast towards the Sea of Japan, the South Korean and Japanese militaries said, six days after a similar North Korean short-range ballistic missile launch on August 6.

Trump may be trying to improve relations with Kim, said Jenny Town, head of the Stimson Center think ‌tank’s 38 ⁠North program.

“This decision may be part of a larger effort to create a diplomatic opportunity with Pyongyang, as Trump has consistently wanted since coming back to office, although the haphazard nature of this move is unlikely to make much of an impression in Pyongyang,” Town said in an email.

The relationship between Trump and Kim has been a roller coaster for years.

Trump once mocked the North Korean leader as “little rocket man” and threatened Pyongyang with “fire and fury,” while Kim boasted that he would “tame the mentally deranged US dotard with fire.”

Yet they also took part in three summits, with Trump declaring, “we fell in love” after exchanging letters with Kim. None of these efforts led to changes in North ⁠Korea’s nuclear weapons or ballistic missile development.

Even as Trump on Sunday spoke warmly of nuclear-armed North Korea, he pointed to South Korea’s stance on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.

“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’“ Trump wrote.

Exercises shift to simulations

It’s unclear how the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills could be cut back, but in ⁠recent years, they have shifted away from live-fire exercises to computer-simulated missile and cyberattacks.

US military officials have said that North Korean troops, who have fought alongside Russia in its invasion of Ukraine, have gained experience from the conflict, including the growing use of unmanned systems, electronic warfare and cyber operations.

Ukraine said last week that North Korean-made missiles were used in a Russian ballistic missile attack on a steel plant in ⁠Zaporizhzhia that killed seven workers and forced a production halt, with Russia’s Zircon hypersonic missiles also used in the attack.

A high-ranking US Northern Command official, Lieutenant General Joseph Jarrard, last week warned that North Korea had successfully tested intercontinental ballistic missiles with “enough boost to deliver a nuclear payload anywhere in North America,” complicating US homeland defence efforts.

articles.title: At Re-Kriti, the product is the hero
articles.summary:
Growing up in New Road, one of Kathmandu’s busiest shopping hubs, Nasana Bajracharya watched her neighbourhood change around her.

Stores that once sold food, electronics, and other goods gradually became clothing shops. By the time she finished school, she remembers seeing clothes almost everywhere she looked.

It left her with a question. “Who wears these many clothes?” she wondered. And if people were buying so much, what happened to everything they no longer wore?

During the second year of her BBA, she participated in a startup idea competition. When asked to come up with a business idea, textile upcycling was the first thing that came to her.

That idea eventually became Re-Kriti.

Four years into its work, Re-Kriti has upcycled around 2,200 kilograms of jeans. More than 700 customers have handed over their old jeans to be transformed into bags. The organisation has also provided income-generating opportunities to 11 women artisans.

But getting people to see an old pair of jeans as raw material rather than rubbish has not always been easy.

“People did think that products made from discarded fabric are of low quality,” she says. Some expected products to cost between Rs200 and Rs500 simply because the material had already been used. The reasoning was: If it is old, why should I pay much for it?

For Bajracharya, Nepal’s textile waste problem cannot be separated from the fast-fashion industry. Clothing stores have multiplied, online shopping has expanded, and people are consuming more clothes without necessarily using what they already own.

And getting rid of clothes does not necessarily solve the problem either. Donation is often treated as an easy answer to unwanted clothing. But Re-Kriti’s founder argues that donating transfers the responsibility if there is no demand for what is being given.

Charity and thrift stores can also accumulate clothing that nobody wants, leaving the problem unresolved.

At Re-Kriti, however, clothes that have already reached that point are given another possibility.

Some materials arrive from garment factories, where unused fabric may be discarded despite being new. Others are purchased from thrift stores that have been unable to sell them. Customers also bring in their own old jeans.

Used denim is washed, sorted and eventually cut and stitched into new products. During its early days, the team could use only around 60 to 70 percent of a pair of jeans.

Today, the founder estimates that around 95 percent of each pair can be upcycled. Pockets and smaller pieces can become wallets, key rings and bag charms. She says only a few sections, such as the zipper and upper belt portion, remain difficult to repurpose.

Working with waste, it turns out, requires learning how to waste less of it.

The organisation deliberately works with local women artisans, particularly home-based tailors. Women may receive sewing and other vocational training through municipalities, wards, and different programmes, but learning a skill does not guarantee having somewhere to use it.

Household and caregiving responsibilities can make conventional working hours difficult. And when women cannot commit to a 10-to-6 job, formal employment opportunities shrink.

Re-Kriti therefore designed part of its production around home-based work, sending quality-checked materials to the artisans.

Of the 11 women who have received income opportunities through Re-Kriti, six currently receive consistent work, while five others are engaged when production increases.

She remembers one home-based tailor who had previously been poorly paid and treated badly elsewhere but had few alternatives. After beginning to earn through Re-Kriti, the founder says she noticed a change not only in her income but also in her confidence.

The first two years, Bajracharya says, felt like “hitting a wall”.

People sometimes bought Re-Kriti products because they admired the cause. That support was encouraging, but she quickly realised it was not enough to sustain a business.

So Re-Kriti studied online inquiries, marketplace responses and feedback from previous customers to understand what people actually wanted.

That process led to one of the most important lessons Re-Kriti has learned about sustainability.

“The product is the hero,” the founder says.

In the beginning, Re-Kriti emphasised words like ‘upcycled’ and ‘sustainable’. For people already concerned about the environment, that message could be persuasive.

For everyone else, sustainability alone was not enough; the product also had to be attractive and useful.

That realisation pushed Re-Kriti to invest more in product development, marketing and how its work was presented on social media.

Sometimes, however, the old material carries a value that no new fabric could replicate.

One customer had kept a pair of her father’s vintage jeans long after he had stopped wearing them. The jeans no longer suited his style, but she had preserved them anyway.

After discovering Re-Kriti, she sent the jeans three weeks before her birthday and asked the team to turn them into a bag. Along with them came a handwritten note thanking the team for allowing something that belonged to her father to become something she could now carry herself.

Stories like these, Bajracharya says, become “fuel” during periods when sales are poor and she questions why she started the business at all.

Re-Kriti has also tried to take upcycling outside its own production space.

Since 2025, it has organised five ‘Upcycling Mela’ events at colleges. Around 150 students and 20 teachers have participated, either bringing old jeans for Re-Kriti to transform or taking part in upcycling activities themselves.

That participation matters because Bajracharya believes Nepal does not necessarily suffer from a lack of conversations about sustainability.

If anything, she thinks there are too many.

Every Environment Day, every Plastic Free July and at sustainability programmes throughout the year, similar conversations return.

“We are only having conversations,” she says. “We are having too many conversations, honestly.”

What is missing, she argues, is action.

A person may hear repeatedly that overconsumption is harmful, but the idea becomes different when they hold an old pair of jeans, work with it and see it become something useful.

That is also why she believes changing consumer behaviour is more realistic than waiting for the fashion industry to transform itself. Consumers, however, make choices every time they purchase something.

Perhaps that is Re-Kriti’s larger experiment. Its work begins with jeans, but the question it poses is not whether an old pair can become a bag. It is whether people can learn to look at what they already own differently.

A pocket can become a wallet. A scrap can become a key ring. A father’s old jeans can become his daughter’s birthday bag. A skill learned by a home-based tailor can become a source of income.

And a pair of jeans someone was ready to throw away can still have somewhere to go. For Re-Kriti, sustainability begins there.

articles.title: New Kathmandu festival brings Tarkovsky, Kapadia and Nepali cinema together
articles.summary:
‘Licchavi Cinema Festival’ will hold its first edition in Kathmandu from 11 to 15 September 2026 at QFX Cinemas, Chhaya Centre, showcasing a curated programme of feature films from Asia and world cinema.

The festival grows out of Licchavi House’s commitment to cinema and cultural dialogue, as well as filmmaker Khyentse Norbu’s (Founder, Licchavi House) long-standing connection to Nepal.

The inaugural selection brings together films from Nepal, Bhutan, India, Pakistan, Thailand, France, Germany, Japan, and Russia. The programme places contemporary Asian cinema alongside major works from different periods and traditions, including films by Andrei Tarkovsky, Payal Kapadia, Khyentse Norbu, Deepak Rauniyar, Abinash Bikram Shah, and Tashi Gyeltshen.

The films include ‘The Cup’, ‘Elephants in the Fog’, ‘White Sun’, ‘The Red Phallus’, ‘All We Imagine as Light’, ‘Ghost School’, ‘Stalker’, ‘La Haine’, ‘Perfect Days’, and ‘Memoria’.

“What we are doing with this first edition is placing our own cinema in conversation with the world,” says Abishek Budhathoki, festival curator, Licchavi Cinema Festival. “Cinema literacy is not a specialist skill. It belongs to any audience willing to engage. We envision Licchavi Cinema to be part of that growth, and open to anyone who wants in.”

The festival takes the Garuda as its emblem to protect what is lasting in cinema, and to carry it toward audiences who might not otherwise encounter it. In Nepal, and across Buddhist and Hindu traditions, the Garuda is a protector and messenger, a figure that moves between realms and carries word from one to the other, belonging fully to neither sky nor earth.

The ‘Licchavi Cinema Festival’ will be held with the support of Kathmandu Metropolitan City and the European Union.

Licchavi Cinema Festival

When: 11 to 15 September

Where: QFX Cinemas, Chhaya Center, Thamel

Time: Will be released soon

Entry: Tickets will be available soon on Khalti

articles.title: Shusmita Thapa Magar begins her pro MMA journey with win
articles.summary:
Shusmita Thapa Magar has already tested her might at Muay Thai and kickboxing. Now, she has started her pro mixed martial arts journey in style: she registered a win in her debut.

Magar defeated India’s Shalu Sharma by unanimous decision at a co-main event at Ronin Fighting Championship-3 in Bengaluru on Saturday night.

Magar, who has a pro Muay Thai record of 7-0 and a pro kickboxing record of 2-2, had previously fought at Ronin Fighting Championship-2. However, it was in kickboxing and she had defeated Aarti Khatri, again by unanimous decision.

Magar seemed to be enjoying her fight against Sharma, who had an upper hand in grappling. However, Magar found her way around and used Sharma’s grappling against her.

Out of the three rounds of five minutes each, Magar dominated all three. In the second round, Magar had Sharma on the mat for most of the time and kept pounding with her elbow. Sharma even got a cut on her eyebrow.

The punches continued in the third round as well.

The only thing Magar seemed dissatisfied with was she was not able to knock her opponent out.

articles.title: Indian Army chief Dhiraj Seth arrives in Kathmandu for four-day visit
articles.summary:
Indian Army chief General Dhiraj Seth arrived in Kathmandu on Sunday for a four-day visit at the invitation of Nepal’s Chief of the Army Staff General Ashok Sigdel.

Seth arrived at Tribhuvan International Airport at 4:15pm on an Air India flight. Senior Nepali Army officials were at the airport to receive him.

According to Nepali Army officials, during his stay, Seth is most likely to hold meetings with Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who also oversees the Defence Ministry, and General Sigdel, among other senior officials.

President Ramchandra Paudel, who is also the supreme commander of the Nepali Army, is scheduled to confer on Seth the honorary rank of General of the Nepali Army at a special ceremony at the President’s Office on Monday, said Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, spokesperson for the Nepali Army.

Nepal and India have a longstanding tradition of conferring the honorary rank of general on each other’s army chiefs. The practice began in 1950 and is regarded by both sides as a symbol of the close and mutually respectful ties between the two countries.

Under the tradition, Nepal’s army chief is conferred the honorary rank of General of the Indian Army, while the Indian Army chief receives the honorary rank of General of the Nepali Army.

Seth, who took charge as Indian Army chief on June 30, will also attend other events organised by the Nepali Army during his visit.

Seth is the first senior Indian official to visit Nepal since the formation of the Balendra Shah government on March 27. Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri had earlier been scheduled to visit Kathmandu, but his trip was postponed over protocol-related issues.

General Sigdel was conferred the honorary rank of General of the Indian Army by Indian President Droupadi Murmu in December 2024.

articles.title: Death toll from Jajarkot landslide rises to four
articles.summary:
The death toll from a landslide in Jajarkot’s Bheri Municipality-2 has risen to four after the body of a man who had been missing since Saturday evening was recovered, police said.

The body of 70-year-old Bhim Bahadur Karki was found buried in the landslide about 50 metres below his home, according to police.

Earlier, 52-year-old Kedar Karki, who was injured in the landslide, died while being taken to Nepalgunj for treatment.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Buddhisagar Puri of the Jajarkot District Police Office said the bodies of 54-year-old Om Singh Khatri and his mother, Rati Khatri, had also been recovered from the landslide.

Puri said Om Singh and Rati had been missing since Saturday evening.

articles.title: Five nominees unveiled for NSJF Pulsar Sports Award
articles.summary:
The Nepal Sports Journalists Forum on Thursday announced five athletes representing five different sports disciplines as the nominees for the People’s Choice category at the 23rd edition of the Pulsar Sports Award.

The list includes volleyball spiker Meena Sunar, footballer Puja Rana, karateka Sanu Maya Thing, cricketer Sher Malla, and mixed martial arts fighter Rabindra Dhant. The winner will be determined through public voting and announced during the main awards ceremony scheduled for September 3 (Bhadra 18).

The players were selected by a committee led by NSJF secretary Anil Malla Thakuri. The other members were AIPS-ASIA’s treasurer Niranjan Rajbanshi, Himesh Ratna Bajracharya, Prajeet Shakya and Birat Jung Rayamajhi.

About the nominees

Sunar is an emerging volleyball star. She captained Everest Volleyball Club and led Nepal Police Club to a third-place finish at the CAVA Women’s Club Championship. Internationally, she earned a silver medal at the CAVA U19 Championship in Sri Lanka and a bronze at the CAVA U20 Championship in the Maldives.

Rana, a key defender, delivered standout performances during the Asian Cup Qualifiers in Uzbekistan last year. She has also established a strong overseas profile, playing in professional leagues for Transport United in Bhutan, as well as Farashganj FC and Nasrin Sports Academy in Bangladesh.

Karateka Thing secured team kata gold and individual kata silver at the South Asian Karate Championship. She represented Nepal at the World Karate Championship in Cairo and claimed gold at the UKKS One Ultimate Kata and Kumite Challenge.

Malla, an off-spinner, took a wicket on his very first ball during his ICC T20 World Cup debut against England in February. He earned his national team call-up following a standout campaign with Lumbini Lions in the Nepal Premier League Season 2, having previously won the inaugural NPL title with Janakpur Bolts. He also captained Sudurpashchim Province to the Prime Minister Cup final.

Meanwhile, Dhant, who has earned the moniker ‘Bajhang ko Bagh’, made history as the first Nepali fighter to enter the “Road to UFC” tournament. Having won his opening fight in May, he is currently sharpening his skills at Bali-based Soma Fight Club ahead of his next bout in Shanghai on August 28. Dhant also claimed the bantamweight title at Matrix Fight Night 17 in India by defeating Chungreng Koren.

Voting mechanics

Along with unveiling the nominees, the NSJF announced a major shift in the category's voting mechanics.

Renewing its sponsorship agreement with 'Khalti By IME' as the official digital voting partner, the forum announced that fans will no longer have to pay to cast their votes.

Under the new model, the public can cast one free vote daily for their preferred athlete until 11:59 pm on September 2.

“The voting process was revised to address concerns that athletes with wealthier fan bases previously held an unfair advantage,” said NSJF President Niranjan Adhikari. “We believe this format levels the playing field.”

Votes cast via the Khalti app will account for 50 percent of the total score. The remaining 50 percent will be evaluated through votes from NSJF members, national chief coaches, and public interaction on the official Facebook pages of the NSJF Pulsar Sports Award and Pulsar Nepal.

The winner of the People’s Choice Award will receive a Pulsar motorcycle. Winners across the remaining categories—including Para Athlete, Special Award, Lifetime Achievement, and Asian Sports Journalist—will receive Rs100,000 each.

articles.title: Minister Lamsal to return to Kathmandu after falling ill in Baitadi
articles.summary:
Physical Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal is returning to Kathmandu by helicopter after falling ill during a field visit to Baitadi, officials said.

Meena Aryal, chief district officer of Baitadi, said arrangements had been made for a helicopter to take Lamsal to Kathmandu.

“The coordination for the helicopter has been completed. It may have already taken off,” Aryal said.

Doctors at the District Hospital Baitadi said an initial examination showed symptoms of a viral infection and common cold.

“We found symptoms of a viral infection and common cold. We believe excessive travel and changes in weather may have contributed to his condition,” Dr Pabin Upadhyay said. “His condition cannot be determined conclusively without a detailed medical examination.”

Lamsal had travelled through Kailali, BP Nagar in Doti, Dadeldhura and Darchula before reaching Baitadi. He was scheduled to travel to Bajhang on Sunday.

His planned visits to Bajhang and other districts have been postponed, Aryal said.

Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) activist Nitis Joshi, who is accompanying the minister’s team, said Lamsal was also scheduled to visit Bajura and Achham.

Lamsal is travelling with ministry secretary Gopal Sigdel, the director generals of four departments under the ministry, including those responsible for water supply, roads, urban development and building construction, and local infrastructure development, along with members of his secretariat and some RSP leaders.

articles.title: Twelve killed and at least 10 injured in Polish bus crash in Hungary
articles.summary:
A dozen people were killed and at least 10 injured ​after a Polish bus overturned at night on a motorway ‌in eastern Hungary, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday morning in a Facebook post.

The bus ran into a ditch and tipped over early on Sunday ​near the town of Mezokeresztes in eastern Hungary, police said, ​adding that the bus was heading towards the city of Nyiregyhaza on the motorway when the accident happened.

State news agency MTI ​said there were 57 passengers and two drivers on the bus. Pictures ​from the scene showed a badly damaged red bus lying on one side in a ditch by the motorway with windows smashed and belongings and suitcases scattered ​around.

“A Polish-registered bus travelling on the M3 motorway towards Nyiregyhaza ... veered ​off the straight stretch of road into a ditch and overturned. Preliminary information suggests ‌the driver likely fell asleep,” police said on their website.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said on X: “It is with deep sorrow that I received the tragic news of the Polish bus accident in Hungary, in which so ​many of our ​compatriots died.”

Twelve ⁠people lost their lives, and several others were injured in the accident, police said, adding that they were ​taking the bus driver into custody.

The injured have been ​taken to hospital.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on X that a “tragic accident” involving a bus carrying Polish tourists happened in Hungary.

“The consular service is operational. ⁠We ​are in contact with the Hungarian authorities. ​The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will provide verified information,” he said.

articles.title: Non-resident Nepalis keen on domestic ventures, but cite bureaucratic hurdles and safety fears
articles.summary:
Non-resident Nepalis have expressed strong interest in investing in Nepal, but say cumbersome legal procedures, excessive bureaucracy, political instability and concerns over economic security continue to discourage capital inflows.

Delegates attending the ongoing 11th Asia-Pacific Regional Conference of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) in Guangzhou, China, urged the government to simplify regulations and create a more predictable environment for investment.

Former NRNA president Binod Kunwar, a businessman based in South Korea, said a gap between government rhetoric and implementation remains a major obstacle to investment.

“I have equal investments in both Nepal and South Korea. My experience shows that Nepal suffers from too much talk and too little work,” Kunwar said. “We must formulate time-bound plans. Execution must take place on schedule; otherwise, efforts yield no results. Moreover, adequate execution time must be allotted.”

Kunwar said outdated and restrictive legal requirements often make it difficult for entrepreneurs to operate efficiently, while lengthy administrative procedures add to the cost of doing business.

“Wherever regulatory hurdles exist, the government must intervene immediately to facilitate operations. Furthermore, bank interest rates in Nepal remain exorbitantly high,” he said, calling for a review of monetary and regulatory policies.

Former NRNA president Upendra Mahato said Nepalis living abroad closely follow Nepal’s development and many want to contribute to it. He urged the government to view that sentiment as an economic opportunity.

“Nepal will ultimately be built by Nepalis themselves. If eloquent speeches and sweet promises could build a nation, it would have been prosperous long ago,” Mahato said. “We must now spur development while preserving our heritage and civilisation. That is the resolve we must all make.”

Mahato said diaspora capital alone would not guarantee economic development without clear and investor-friendly laws.

“You cannot attract capital by threatening or intimidating entrepreneurs; you bring in investment by creating a stable environment and offering robust legal protection,” he said. He added that investment by non-resident Nepalis could also help attract wider foreign direct investment by connecting Nepal to international business networks.

NRNA senior vice president Rabin Sherchan said Nepal has significant untapped potential in several sectors and urged non-resident Nepalis to identify emerging areas and increase their investments.

South Korea-based researcher Devi Bahadur Basnet said Nepal could offer opportunities for innovation in medical and protein science.

“There are abundant opportunities to pioneer new ventures in Nepal. We must actively search for them,” Basnet said, adding that Nepal’s natural environment could offer advantages for medical research and related investment.

But infrastructure constraints, particularly along Nepal’s northern border, continue to hamper trade and manufacturing.

Nirmal Sharma Chaulagai, former president of NRNA China, said inadequate infrastructure at border points with China was limiting trade.

He said traders were currently able to import goods through northern border points for only about six months a year because of inadequate facilities.

“Because the government fails to construct infrastructure on time, industrialists suffer severe financial losses as consignment cargoes remain stranded at border checkpoints for extended periods,” Chaulagai said.

Another former president of NRNA China, Rohit Agrawal, said investors ultimately needed assurance that their investments would generate reasonable returns.

Such assurances, he said, required clear statutory protections. Pointing to China, Agrawal said its pragmatic governance and emphasis on economic security had helped attract global capital and offered lessons for Nepal.

Arun Kumar Subedi, a researcher on investment issues, criticised the bureaucratic hurdles faced by investors in Nepal. He said entrepreneurs investing billions of rupees still had to deal with routine administrative problems at the hands of junior government officials.

Citing research, Subedi said around 40 percent of Nepalis living abroad wanted to invest in Nepal, but political instability remained a major deterrent.

Officiating Ambassador of Nepal to China Roshan Khanal assured the delegates that the embassy was ready to help identify viable investment opportunities.

Khanal said 61 percent of Nepalis who had established successful enterprises in China had expressed a strong desire to return to Nepal and set up businesses there.

Former parliamentarian and Nepali Communist Party leader Madhav Sapkota said the discussion on attracting diaspora investment should extend beyond initial capital. He called for greater attention to ways of converting Nepal’s large remittance inflows into productive, long-term investment.

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Khagendra Sunar said his party was committed to creating a more favourable investment climate, with the objective outlined in its election manifesto.

“In the past, Nepal had a culture where instead of promoting shoe manufacturing, people ended up dismantling the manufacturing companies themselves,” Sunar said. “However, that practice must end, and the government is committed to ending it. We invite you to come and invest. As parliamentarians, we stand fully prepared to draft whatever legislative frameworks are required.”

articles.title: Your skin needs a Nepal-specific routine for its climate, altitude and pollution
articles.summary:
There is much noise alongside some genuine information on the internet about how to take care of one’s skin. Information on the internet comes from people all over the world and may often not be applicable to Nepal. Given its climate, altitude, and specific problems such as urban pollution, people’s needs will differ and require tailored solutions.

Dr Shreya Bastakoti is a consultant dermatologist and cosmetic surgeon at Lavana Skin and Hair Clinic in Kathmandu, Nepal. She obtained her MD in dermatology from Kathmandu University and received aesthetic training in Bangkok and Mumbai.

Bastakoti, who provides aesthetic services to patients with diverse dermatological concerns, discusses common skincare problems in Nepal and how people can adapt their routines to the country’s varied climate, altitude, and seasons.

What are the issues that people living specifically in Nepal face in terms of skincare?

Skin concerns in Nepal vary significantly depending on geography, altitude, climate, and lifestyle.

In the mountainous regions, low temperatures, dry air, strong winds, and high UV exposure can lead to dry and sensitive skin, chapped lips, sunburn, pigmentation, premature ageing, and, in severe conditions, frostbite.

In urban areas such as Kathmandu, air pollution is an important concern. Prolonged exposure to pollutants can disrupt the skin barrier and contribute to dryness, irritation, acne, pigmentation, and premature skin ageing.

In the Tarai and warmer, humid regions, heat, sweating, and friction create favourable conditions for fungal infections, intertrigo, folliculitis, acne, and heat rashes.

How does the monsoon season affect these problems compared to the dry season?

The monsoon season, with its high humidity and increased environmental moisture, can significantly influence several skin conditions. The warm, humid climate creates an ideal environment for fungal growth, leading to an increase in fungal infections, pityriasis versicolor, and intertrigo.

Increased sweating and occlusion may also contribute to acne and folliculitis flare-ups. Additionally, people may experience more allergic reactions, including those triggered by pollen, insects, and environmental allergens.

In contrast, the dry season generally has lower humidity, resulting in fewer fungal and moisture-related skin problems, although dryness, irritation, and skin-barrier disruption may become more prominent. Overall, skincare needs to be adapted according to the seasonal climate.

What is the importance of sunscreen in the high altitudes and plains in Nepal?

Sunscreen is an essential part of skincare throughout Nepal, particularly because of the country’s significant variation in altitude and consistently high levels of ultraviolet (UV) exposure.

At high altitudes, UV radiation is stronger because the atmosphere provides less filtration, and exposure is further intensified by reflection from snow and other surfaces. This increases the risk of sunburn, pigmentation, premature skin ageing, and cumulative UV-induced skin damage. Therefore, regular use of a broad-spectrum, high-SPF sunscreen is particularly important for people living at or travelling to higher elevations.

In the plains and lower-altitude regions, although UV intensity may differ, prolonged exposure to strong sunlight remains an important concern. Sunscreen helps prevent tanning, pigmentation, photoaging, and long-term UV-related skin damage.

How can people take good care of their skin in these circumstances?

I always believe that good skincare is about keeping it simple and being consistent, rather than using many products. You do not necessarily need an elaborate 10-step routine to maintain healthy skin. The basics—a gentle face wash, a moisturiser suited to your skin type, and a broad-spectrum sunscreen—are often enough for most people.

The routine should also be adapted to the environment. In cold, dry or high-altitude areas, a richer moisturiser and regular lip balm can help protect the skin barrier. In hot and humid regions, lighter, non-comedogenic products may be more comfortable and help reduce excess oil and sweating. Sunscreen should be used daily, especially when there is significant sun exposure, and reapplied when outdoors for prolonged periods.

Most importantly, avoid constantly changing products or following every skincare trend. Healthy skin comes from the right products, used regularly and appropriately for your individual skin needs

articles.title: Fiction: So, you want to be a leader?
articles.summary:
Whenever the Chasmey Poet posted his creations on Facebook, speculation brewed in Deshbhumi. The general public would applaud how the poet had stabbed the leaders with his sharp and witty words. Leaders and their loyalists would scrunch their noses in utter disgust. For a day or two, the poem overtook the political gossip in teashops and chautaris.

“He has always been vocal when it comes to pointing out the ills.”

“He is born to write.”

“If he corrects his ways and writes in a milder tone, the state will recognise his talent. Might even get the title of ‘Thulo Kabi’ someday.”

Among these commentators, some frustrated men would astound the circle with their eccentric logic.

“Imagine such a young man in politics. He knows where the problem lies. Wouldn’t it be amazing to have him as our PM?”

Soon, people around would take their time to imagine Chasmey Poet sitting in the PM’s chair, sober, restless, and dedicated to serving Deshbhumi’s citizenry.

On the top floor of his house, in his crammed room, Chasmey Poet sat on the bed and readied himself for another striking poem. From the window of his room, Kathland—the capital of Deshbhumi—looked hazy, its hustle and bustle getting to the poet, who quietly chronicled it and its operators.

As he got up from the bed to look for an ashtray, he checked himself in the mirror and, smiling, took off his dark shades. Had he slept with his shades on? Over the years, the dark glasses had become his signature style, and without even realising it, he wore them everywhere.

He liked that young people in Kathland had started buying shades to imitate his style. What was once a trick to shield his bloodshot eyes, he recalled, had become an iconic style among Deshbhumi’s youth.

Now, as he gained popularity, he was less worried about his parents finding out about his smoking habit. What did it matter as long as he could compose poems that rattled the powerful chairs in Deshbhumi? The more the Sarkar missed the mark, the more the Chasmey Poet gained—fame, name, and money. It was as if all the Chasmey Poet did was wait for the Sarkar to falter.

After snuffing out the cigarette, he sat at his desk, where papers were strewn about. A minute or two passed in fruitless imagination. In the last few days, he hadn’t paid much attention to political matters. After posting on his Facebook wall a few days ago, he hadn’t opened the apps, not even once.

Now, as he struggled with words, he realised that he should stop binge-watching web series and focus more on Facebook—where political updates were frequent, and leaders made important announcements. And what about his all-knowing friends? Why hadn’t they come to his house or invited him over for a quick tea chat? He should plan a meeting at Chiya Ghar, where his friends often congregated, with politics always at the center of attention.

As he impatiently waited for the evening, he smoked more and scrolled through his old posts—blatant accusations of the Sarkar’s wrongdoings. His latest post—a sharp poem accusing the Sarkar of turning a deaf ear to the farmers’ plight—had garnered thousands of likes, with some of his die-hard fans even commenting, “Gajendra aau, desh bachau.”

Accustomed to hearing “Chasmey Poet,” he felt like a different person when people called him Gajendra. The Sarkar—as ruthless as it could get—had repeatedly delayed the payment to sugarcane farmers from the southern plains. As if reciting the old poem would inspire a new one, the poet read out the last lines:

“They have given loads of sugar, And in exchange, The Sarkar is robbing them of the salt.”

In the evening, at Chiya Ghar, the poet and his friends occupied a table in a far corner, where no one could overhear them. If someone caught a whiff of their conversation, it could be bad for their reputation, especially the poet’s.

Not only the poet but his friends—both of them—were also leveraging the internet to a great extent. In the country full of bumpkins, earning dollars through the internet was nothing short of pure brilliance.

“Have you gone through the comments on your last post?” Mr Gaudel asked and looked at Gajendra, who was already lighting a cigarette.

“Yeah, yeah, I did this morning. All that useless stuff about how I should lead Deshbhumi,” he coughed, unable to contain his laughter.

“People are so frustrated, I can see that,” Kunwar—the owner of a low-key meme page—said in a low voice.

“They keep making mistakes. Look at the count on my Facebook wall. And look at their pleas. People think I should replace them,” said the poet and snickered like it was the best joke of the evening.

“But I think we are underestimating ourselves, guys. I’m not talking about myself. I am also unsure about Gaudel, but Gajendra has a real chance in politics.” Kunwar was serious, his eyes darting between his friends.

Gajendra could dismiss this. It was not the first time Kunwar was trying to lure his poet friend into politics. What did he actually see in Gajendra? What did he know besides composing poems?

“Why don’t you join a party and start on your own, Kunwar?” the poet asked his friend, who, cupping his chin, said, “Because I’m not as popular as you are.”

“Hello, waiter? Get us three bottles of beer with three glasses,” Gaudel ordered, finding it important to keep the momentum going. There was no objection from the other end.

“If you look at the pattern in politics, it’s actually the opposite in our case. First the post, then popularity,” Kunwar looked at Gaudel and asked, “Isn’t it right?”

Gaudel nodded, adding, “The main thing is popularity, and people already like how you go against the Sarkar every time.”

“And what about us? You think we can’t influence people? People wait for my page’s posts to make sense of what’s happening every day,” Gaudel said, gauging the poet, who already looked submissive and deep in thought.

“Make me your secretary and watch how I supply you with the knowledge,” Kunwar winked, raising his glass for the toast.

“You guys are seriously pushing me into trouble,” the poet laughed, but solemnly, as if the anticipation already weighed on him.

The three of them enjoyed the beer in the cool evening as people flocked in and out of the restaurant. Although curtains were drawn from every side, they could hear the murmurs in the distance. As the three kept themselves busy with their talks, the murmurs in the distance grew into castigations.

Kunwar gathered it quickly and explained it to his friends. “See, this is about the minister’s statement. Today, one of the ministers in the cabinet called Deshbhumi’s youths useless and phone-addicted.”

Gaudel was aware of this, but the poet had no clue.

“The minister was even suggesting putting some sort of restriction on social media. Totally absurd,” Gaudel remarked.

Within a second, Kunwar exploded. “The youths on social media have announced that they are staging nationwide protests against the Sarkar. You know what? This is the right time for us.”

Drunk and furious, the poet thought of the minister and struggled to find the right words to start the poem. Kunwar—who was eyeing the poet all the while—was puzzled because the poet looked lost.

“Gajendra, I need your phone right now,” it was Kunwar.

“What for?”

“Okay, okay, I don’t need it. But write yourself.”

Now, the poet understood what Kunwar was implying, and for a split second, in his drunken state, he felt like calling him by this name: “The Mastermind Kunwar.”

“It’s hard to think of a poem now, especially in this drunken state,” Gajendra said, baffled as his friends watched him expectantly.

“Ah, see! We can’t wait for your brain to click with the poem,” Kunwar heaved a sigh.

“Just put up a status directly, or let me do it for you,” Gaudel was equally irritated now.

The urgency perplexed the poet. These friends, he thought, knew better about the internet, and perhaps even politics.

“Here, do whatever the hell you want,” Chasmey Poet pushed his phone towards Kunwar. The poet was on his seventh glass of beer.

It took only two minutes for Kunwar to think of and write the post on the poet’s wall. It read:

“We are governed by goons who think our youth are useless. I fully support your protest against the Sarkar. Go and teach them a lesson.”

That was it. People went berserk on Facebook, sharing the post, commenting on it, and cursing fiercely at the Sarkar. Everyone began to chant Gajendra’s name as he busied himself with more drinking.

But Mastermind Kunwar knew the intensity of the status and what it could do in Deshbhumi tomorrow. At worst, he knew, the Sarkar would buckle under the pressure of the protesting youths. Others had no clue, not even Gajendra. But Kunwar knew that this was only the beginning, and his orchestration would have to grow bolder as politics evolved in Deshbhumi.

articles.title: From cinema halls to social media: How Nepali films are facing a new piracy threat
articles.summary:
When Suman Giri, one of the producers of Nepal’s third-highest grossing film ‘Gauthali’, came across a YouTube channel that had been continuously posting pirated clips of his movie, what struck him was more than the piracy itself. It was a weary reminder of human nature.

With clips ranging from a few seconds to hours being recorded inside cinema halls and circulated without copyright permission, Giri, also one of the co-producers of Nepal’s most celebrated franchise ‘Chakka Panja’, now believes that every Nepali film is vulnerable to digital piracy.

Initially, he said, short clips of one or two minutes from ‘Gauthali’ were shared, which the production house tolerated since they also served as promotion. But almost inevitably, it escalated to 20, 27, and even 30-minute segments, splitting the film into ‘Part 1, Part 2’.

“This was when we were compelled to report the materials to the Cyber Bureau,” he said. “Almost 300 clips posted on social media, particularly on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, have been taken down until now.”

Nepali cinema is increasingly facing sophisticated digital piracy, yet the country's response remains merely reactive. The legal actions involve taking down individual clips under laws that predate the current social-media ecosystem, without even knowing the scale of the losses.

With this trend of digital piracy, the Nepal Film Development Board issued a notice on July 31, 2026, urging social media users and digital platform operators to stop the unauthorised recordings of Nepali and foreign film screenings in theatres.

The Board warned that such ‘cam-recording’ violated Nepal’s Copyright Act 2002 and Electronic Transactions Act 2006, further calling on the public to remove any illegally recorded content posted online. It cautioned that those involved in unauthorised recording or piracy could face legal action under existing law.

The Copyright Act (2002) declares that reproducing, distributing, or publicly sharing a film without the copyright owner’s authorisation constitutes infringement. Offenders, as a result, can face a fine of Rs10,000 to Rs100,000, or imprisonment of up to six months, or both, along with seizure of the pirated materials and compensation to the copyright owner.

In accordance with the existing laws, the Nepal Police’s Cyber Bureau handles complaints that require digital evidence such as screenshots, URLs, transaction IDs, and metadata-preserved chat logs.

“We have received digital piracy complaints particularly from the films ‘Gauthali’ and ‘Balidan’,” said Dilip Kumar Giri, SP at the Bureau. “After receiving the links to the illegally uploaded movie clips, we have been taking them down from social media.”

Yet, many Nepali audiences appear unaware that recording, sharing, or distributing copyrighted material without permission can have legal consequences. For some, watching pirated clips has simply become a way of staying connected to Nepali cinema.

Sona (name changed), an international student, said that watching Nepali films helps her “feel closer to home while staying connected to her language and culture”. As Nepali films are not always screened in global theatres, she turned to pirated videos.

“When I did have the chance to watch movies in the hall, I had posted videos on my Instagram, which I later deleted after realising it was a violation of copyright law.”

The Film Development Board, therefore, steps in to raise awareness, reminding the audience that even casual sharing of pirated clips carries legal consequences.

“Some people may not even know it's wrong, and might post something without any real intention of causing harm,” said Santosh Babu Lohani, board member of the Nepal Film Development Board. “That is why our first and primary focus is on raising awareness.”

As a filmmaker and director himself, Lohani reflects on the challenges of resisting digital piracy.

“I understand that seeing your film scattered across social media in pieces is enormously stressful,” he added.

Before watching any film in cinema halls, the audience comes across a message stating that piracy is illegal and that punishment awaits those who engage in it. These acts, to some extent, serve as an alarm and a warning to mitigate the losses faced by filmmakers.

“There have been cases of an entire film being leaked,” says Lohani. “Losses can range from small amounts to running into the tens of millions.”

While ‘Gauthali’ was able to generate commendable revenue despite the cases, not all Nepali films’ box office could be as ambitious. Digital piracy inflicts direct financial harm on producers, actors, technicians, and exhibitors, while undermining the broader growth of the Nepali film industry.

Meanwhile, other countries are developing technological and institutional responses while Nepal lacks even basic data on the scale of the problem.

As per a recent study, the Indian entertainment industry loses approximately Rs358.4 billion (INR 224 billion) annually to piracy. India’s copyright protection framework—the Copyright Act, 1957 (amended in 2012)—reinforces regulations governing the preservation of digital content. It can lead to imprisonment of up to three years with fines, website blocking, and criminal prosecution under the Copyright Act and the Information Technology Act.

The Japanese government is taking a tech-driven approach to fighting anime and manga piracy. The country’s Agency for Cultural Affairs has set aside roughly 2 million dollars to build an AI-powered system that hunts down and removes pirated content online.

In Nepal, there is neither an official figure tracking the film industry’s monetary losses due to piracy nor a specific aggregation of the official actions taken against it to date.

The question, however, is whether copyright laws written nearly two decades ago remain adequate for a radically transformed digital landscape.

“We are in the process of making a new copyright act,” said Sunita Aryal, Legal officer of Nepal Copyright Registrar’s Office.

Beyond these legal frameworks and revenue losses, digital piracy also comes at the cost of the filmmakers’ faith and trust in their audience. “If something is someone’s intellectual creation, their life’s work and entire income invested into it, and others illegally upload it just so people can watch it for free before it's even properly out, that simply hurts,” says Giri.
